The origins of coffee as a drink involve several stages described across the retrieved sources. Early on, coffee beans were eaten rather than drunk — East African tribes mixed ground coffee cherries with animal fat, and around 1000 AD Ethiopians made a type of wine from fermented coffee berries [d2]. In the 13th century, people began heating or roasting the beans, which is described as "the first step in making coffee as we know it today" [d8]. Coffee was first developed into a hot drink on the Arabian Peninsula, specifically in Yemen, during the 11th century according to one source [d2], while a high-credibility academic source from UC Irvine states that "as a drink, coffee probably dates from the 15th century," with Yemenis being the first to make teas from the coffee fruit and a roasted, ground drink from the bean [d6]. Most historians agree that coffee as a drink first originated from Yemen, in the city of Mocha [d5], and by the 15th–16th centuries it had spread widely across the Middle East [d3][d7]. In short, coffee's transformation into a beverage was gradual, with Yemen playing the central role, and the consensus points to somewhere between the 11th and 15th centuries for when it was first consumed as a drink [d2][d6][d8].
